title: Electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 over dendritic-type Cu- and Fe-based electrodes prepared by electrodeposition
abstract: The identification of the role of nano-morphology of electrodes for the reduction of CO2, particularly in determining the selectivity towards > C1 products of reduction, is still a challenge. We show here for the first time how a dendritic-type nano-morphology and related fractal dimension plays a crucial role in determining the selectivity for electrodes based on Cu and Fe. The electrodes, prepared by electrodeposition of Cu or Fe on metal substrates (Cu, Ti, Al, Fe, Fe-Cr-Ni alloy) or carbon-based gas diffusion layers (GDL), were tested in a continuous flow cell at constant potential (−1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl) or at the onset potential of the first cathodic peak determined by cyclic voltammetry. Results showed that the dendritic-type nano-morphology influences positively not only the activity to formic acid, but especially the selectivity to gas products (i.e. CH4 and CO) and to higher carbon-chain liquid products (i.e. ethanol, isopropanol, acetic acid) when smoother edges and denser surface sites are present. Tests at the onset potential show very high total carbon Faradaic efficiency (FE) for Fe electrodeposited on GDL and Ti (about 92–95%). The lowest onset potential (−0.3 V) is observed for Cu on GDL, showing over 80% total carbon FE and almost 60% FE to formic acid.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The development of electrocatalysts for the reduction of CO2 is a topic of current large research interest [1–8], being a crucial route for CO2 sustainable utilization and climate change mitigation [9,10]. Main focus of the studies has been directed to improve the Faradaic efficiency and understand the reaction mechanism [11,12], with the identification, for example, of metals forming carbon monoxide (Cu, Au, Ag, Zn, Pd, Ga, Ni and Pt) or those forming formic acid/formate (Pb, Hg, In, Sn, Cd and Tl) [13]. Among these electrocatalysts, copper (Cu) represents a special case being able to produce a wide range of products (e.g. methanol, formate, CO) including those involving CeC coupling reaction as key step (e.g. ethylene, ethanol).
However, the understanding of the factors determining the control of the selectivity in CO2 electrocatalytic reduction is still not completed. It has been reported, for example, that the path of the electroreduction of CO2 depends on the crystal faces of Cu nanoparticles or the presence of specific nanostructures such as nanowires [14–16], besides many other parameters including cell design and presence and type of electrolyte [17–19], and surface concentration of CO2 on the electrocatalyst
[20]. The concept that low-dimensional materials are promising candidates for the electrocatalytic CO2 conversion into useful molecules was remarked in many reviews [21], as well as that nanoengineering of the electrodes is a crucial aspect in this reaction [22,23]. However, an important element such as the dendrite-type nanomorphology in the electrocatalyst, which may be associated to the electrode fractal dimension and to the presence of smoother edges and denser surface sites, has been scarcely investigated. We will show here for the first time that this is a crucial aspect to control the Faradaic selectivity in CO2 electrocatalytic materials.
There are limited studies indicating the role of the fractal dimension in influencing the catalytic reactivity of solid materials and even less studies related to electrocatalysts. The fractal dimension in nanometric MoS2 and MoS2/Co catalyst particles was reported as an important factor determining their catalytic behaviour [24] and minimizing the resistances due to Helmholtz double layers [25]. The concept of fractal dimension of electrochemical reactions was introduced by Eftekhari, who correlated the reactive surface area of a catalyst to its surface morphology [26]. However, these studies do not indicate a relationship between fractal dimension and selectivity and were not referring to

These aspects were studied here by using electrocatalysts prepared by electrodeposition of Cu or Fe on different metal substrates or carbonbased gas diffusion layers (GDL), being nanoporous structures prepared by an electrochemical deposition process an area of increasing research interest [29,30]. This method produces what often indicated as nanofoams and various metal/metal-oxide nanofoams (Zn, Sn, Bi, Pb, Ag, Au) have been tested in the CO2 electrocatalytic reaction [31–35], although electrodes based on Cu [36,37] and Fe [38–40] are preferable.
Recently, Kreder and Manthiram produced pure copper metal nanofoams by a facile microwave solvothermal method [41] and Sen et al. showed that copper foams with hierarchical porosity have different performances with respect to smooth electropolished copper electrodes in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 [42]. Kas et al. reported that a hollow fibre copper electrode allows to obtain Faradaic efficiencies for CO2 reduction up to 85% [43]. Dutta et al. showed that highly porous 3D Cu skeletons have Faradaic efficiency of about 30% towards C2 product formation (C2H4, C2H6) in CO2 reduction [44].
Very recently, porous dendritic copper was also reported as an efficient electrocatalyst for CO2 electrocatalytic reduction to formate [45]. A dendrite, an alternative nanostructure which can be produced by electrodeposition, is characterized by a tree-like structure, produced by faster growth along energetically favourable crystallographic directions. Some examples of iron based dendritic nanostructures have also been reported [46–49], but not for the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. While dendritic-type materials and electrodes have been considered separately from nanofoam-type ones, they belong to the same family of materials, but having different fractal dimension.
We have thus investigated here Cu- and Fe-based electrodes prepared by electrodeposition to obtain different fractal dimensions, and a nanostructure ranging from dendritic to nanofoam-type, in order to identify more precisely the role of nanostructure in electrocatalysis for CO2 reduction, and the relation between fractal dimension and nanostructure. These fractal-type active electrocatalysts were grown on different metal substrates (Cu, Fe, Ti, Al and FeCrNi foils, Al grid), as well as over a carbon-based gas diffusion layer (GDL) because the substrate influences significantly the type of nanostructure obtained during electrodeposition.

sections.heading: 2.1. Synthesis of Cu and Fe electrocatalysts
sections.text:
The preparation route of the electrodeposition technique is reported in Scheme 1. Prior to the synthesis, the metal substrates (Cu foil, Ti Foil and Al foil supplied by Sigma Aldrich; Fe foil, Al grid and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, supplied by Good-Fellow) were mechanically polished using a P280 abrasive sheet, then etched using an 0.5M HCl aqueous solution for 5min and finally washed with distilled water and dried. The pretreated substrates were thus used as the cathodes in a two-electrode electrochemical cell, while the anode was a Cu foil, which was pretreated using the same polishing and etching procedure. The two electrodes (cathode and anode) were fixed at a separation distance of 1 cm. A mixture of 0.4M Cu(CH3COO)2, 1.5M H2SO4 and 50mM HCl was used as the electrolyte [50]. The electrochemical deposition of Cu was performed under the application of a constant current (1.2 A) for times of 1, 2 and 4min. After the deposition, the materials were cleaned using distilled water, dried at 80 °C overnight and then calcined at 200 °C (5 °Cmin−1 rate) for 1 h. The final supported Cu electrocatalyst appeared as a dark brown-black electrode. Similarly, Fe electrocatalysts were prepared on Fe, Fe-Cr-Ni alloy and Al substrates using 0.4 M FeSO4 (FeII) as the Fe precursor.
Both Cu and Fe electrocatalysts were also grown on a non-metallic
substrate, i.e. a porous carbon-based gas diffusion layer (GDL, 25 BCE Sigracet® supplied by Ion Power), which was directly used without any treatment. The electrodeposition of electrocatalysts over GDL followed the same procedure reported above, except for the pH of the electrolyte that was adjusted to about 12–13 by adding 1M NaOH. A constant current of 1.2 A was applied for times of 0.5, 1, 2 and 4min.
Iron electrocatalysts were also deposited over Ti substrate applying a constant current of 1.2 A for short electrodeposition times of 15, 30, 45 and 90 s. These smaller times were adopted to evaluate the early stage of crystal growth of Fe electrocatalysts. Two different iron precursors were used: i) FeSO4 (FeII) or Fe2(SO4)3 (FeIII). However, in this case HCl was replaced with HF to improve etching on Ti. Only for the case of Cu electrocatalysts on Fe foils, no current was applied during electrodeposition. In this case, Cu electrocatalysts were grown taking advantage of the favourable reduction potential difference between Cu and Fe. A summary of the electrodes prepared and their acronym used here is given in Table 1.

sections.heading: 2.2. Characterization techniques
sections.text:
The morphology and structure of the Cu and Fe electrocatalysts were studied by a Phenom ProX Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) equipped with EDS analyser.
A D2 Phaser Bruker diffractometer equipped with a Ni β-filtered CuKα radiation source, operating at 30 kV and 10mA, was used to perform X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) analysis, in order to investigate the phase composition and crystalline size of the electrocatalysts. In detail, data were collected in a 2θ range from 12° to 100° at a scanning rate of 0.025° s−1. The JCPDS database of reference compounds was used to identify the diffraction peaks.
The XPS spectra were recorded using a PHI VersaProbe II analyser (Physical Electronics). The results were analysed by using Multipak (Matlab) software. Position of XPS peaks of the corresponding elements was referred to graphite carbon C1s, whose energy was taken equal to 284.8 eV.

sections.heading: 2.3. Electrocatalytic cell for CO2 reduction
sections.text:
The Cu- and Fe-based electrodes were tested as the cathodes in the process of CO2 electrocatalytic reduction. Testing experiments were carried out in a lab-scale device, made in Plexiglas, with a three-electrode configuration. A detailed scheme of the electrochemical cell is reported in Supporting Information. The working electrode (electrocatalyst on metal or GDL substrate) was located into the cathode chamber, close to a reference electrode (Ag/AgCl electrode, 3M KCl, supplied by AMEL), while a Pt rod counter-electrode was placed in the anode hemi-cell. The geometrical surface area of the working electrode was about 5 cm2. A constant voltage of −1.5 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) was applied, if not otherwise reported. A 0.5M KHCO3 aqueous solution was used as the electrolyte in each hemi-cell (catholyte and anolyte). The catholyte solution (25mL) was continuously re-circulated into the cathode from an external container, where 10mLmin−1 CO2 gas flow was used to saturate the catholyte. A buffer CO2/KHCO3 was formed, keeping the pH at about 8.0–8.5. The two compartments were separated by using a proton selective membrane (Nafion 117®, supplied by Ion Power). A potentiostat/galvanostat (AMEL mod. 2049 A) was used to apply the voltage between the electrodes. The liquid products were analysed by Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometer (GC–MS) and Ion Chromatography (IC), while gas products (H2, CH4 and CO) were detected by a Gas Chromatography-Thermal Conductivity-Detector (GCTCD). Further details about the electrocatalytic device were earlier reported [18,51,52]. The same electrochemical cell was used to perform cyclic voltammetry (CV) measurements on the electrodes in the range from −2 V to +2V (vs. Ag/AgCl) with a scan rate of 10 mV s−1.
The Faradaic efficiency (FE) was calculated by Eq. (1):
where n is the number of electrons required for CO2 reduction, F is the Faraday constant, M is the number of moles, I is the average measured current (in Ampere), t is the reaction time (in seconds).

sections.heading: 3.1. Controlling the electrocatalyst nano-dimension
sections.text:
Cu- and Fe-based electrocatalysts with different nanodimension were synthesized using electrodeposition technique. To obtain a more homogeneous set of electrocatalysts, we have changed only the electrodeposition time and type of substrate, while maintaining constant at optimized values other parameters such as the electrolyte, the pH and the potential of deposition. The preparation route of the electrodeposition technique was reported in Scheme 1 of the experimental part. A dendritic-type morphology can be obtained due to H2 bubble formation at high current densities (usually higher than 0.5 A cm−2) [53]. The hydrogen bubbles, formed from the cathodic reaction on the metal substrate, inhibit locally the metal deposition. At the same time,
dendritic fractals derive from nonequilibrium and anisotropic growth [54], due to diffusion-limited [55] and cluster–cluster [56] aggregation effects.
Fig. 1 shows SEM images (top view) of Cu electrocatalysts produced on Cu foils at different electrodeposition times (1, 2 and 4min). After 1min, the presence of a nanofoam-type porous structure and metal agglomerates of 0.3–0.5 μm size can be observed (Fig. 1a). However, a dendritic structure was not formed yet after 1min. Fig. 1b well evidences instead the evolution of the foam into a flake-like structure after 2min of electrodeposition. It resembles a leaf model, with each leaf edge branching into more leaves having a smaller size (about 100 nm). The leaf branches measure sequentially about 3, 5, 8 and finally 13 μm before collapsing due to the increasing weight, as it happened for higher electrodeposition times (i.e. 4 min, as shown in Fig. 1c). The leaf branching approximately follows a Fibonacci sequence (also known as the Golden Ratio), where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones, and which is a common observation in nature from the microscale to the macroscale [57]. The final structure results as dendrites within a connected network of copper pores templated by H2 bubbles. In Supporting Information (SI), a simple geometrical model was used to calculate the total porosity of the foam (50%). An actual foam weight of about 25–30mg was measured by peeling of the foam from the metal base. Moreover, Fig. 1d shows an SEM cross-section image of a Cu sample prepared in 2min, evidencing a thickness of about 20 μm. We will call hereinafter these samples prepared from Cu foils at different electrodeposition times (1, 2 and 4min) as Cu-CFx, where x indicates the electrodeposition time and CF indicates that they are produced from Cu foils. When instead grown over a Fe foil, the acronym is Cu-FFx.
The morphology of copper electrocatalysts strongly depends on the substrate. Fig. 2a and b show two SEM images (top-view) at different magnifications of a Cu electrocatalyst prepared by electrodeposition (2min) using a Fe-Cr-Ni substrate. This sample is called hereinafter CuFCN2, where the suffix 2 indicates 2min of electrodeposition and FCN the Fe-Cr-Ni substrate. A dendritic-like structure is well evidenced, but more compact and closely packed in comparison with the Cu substrate
Scheme 1. Electrodeposition of Cu (or Fe) electrocatalysts on polished metal substrates.
(Fig. 1). The leaf-like model is also different as the leaves look thicker and longer (ranging from 100 nm to 100 μm), forming a dense intricate structure. Fig. 2c and d, instead, refer to Cu electrocatalysts (2 min electrodeposition time) grown on an Al grid as the base substrate. In this case, no dendrites can be observed. The final foam structure is very compact and thick. From the cross-section, a thickness of about 4–5 μm can be measured. This sample is called hereinafter Cu-AG2, where the suffix 2 indicates 2min of electrodeposition and AG the Al Grid substrate.
The morphology is completely different when Cu electrocatalysts were grown on a non-metallic substrate. Fig. 3a shows the SEM top image of Cu electrocatalyst electrodeposited (2min) on a carbon-based substrate (gas diffusion layer – GDL) (Cu-GDL2). It can be well evidenced a network of macropores of about 5–13 μm, with the presence of additional intra-mesopores, but no dendrite-like structures can be observed. By the SEM cross-section of the same sample (Fig. 3b), it is possible to observe that the macropores have a truncated conical hollow structure. In Supporting Information, a simple model of a truncated conical pore was used to calculate the total porosity of the Cu electrocatalyst (about 84%) and the surface area (about 38 cm2 per cm2
of geometrical area). The foam weight was measured to be about 10–15mg by peeling from the GDL substrate. Fig. 3b also shows the foam thickness resulting about 26 μm. By reducing the electrodeposition time to 30 s, the Cu electrocatalyst (Cu-GDL0.5) shows a quite regular urchin-like structure growing until a length of 3 μm (Fig. 3c).
On the contrary, Fe electrocatalysts grown on GDL does not evidence the same urchin-like structure at low electrodeposition time (see Fig. 3d, Fe-GDL0.75). In Supporting Information, further SEM images have been reported (i.e. Fe electrocatalysts on Ti, Al and carbon-based GDL). From SEM analysis, it is evident that electrodeposition time is one of the main parameters influencing the final structure and morphology of the NFs, but this factor is strongly dependent on the nature of the nanofoams.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrocatalyst characterization
sections.text:
EDX measurements evidenced a Cu to O ratio of about 3.4–3.5 depending on the sample (see Supporting Information). A quantitative surface analysis by X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was made to analyse the oxidation state of these Cu electrocatalysts (see
Fig. 1. SEM images of top view of Cu electrocatalysts grown on Cu foils at different electrodeposition times: a) 1min (Cu-CF1), b) 2 min (Cu-CF2) and c) 4 min (CuCF4). Fig. 1d shows a SEM cross-section image of sample Cu-CF2.
Supporting Information). The high-resolution spectrum evidenced two peaks at 932.3 eV and 952.1 eV. They represent the characteristic binding energies for the CuO species, which are further confirmed by satellite peaks at 942.5 eV and 962.6 eV.
X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) was made to determine the crystal structure of Cu electrocatalysts. Fig. 4 shows the XRD patterns of Cu-CF, evidencing a diffraction pattern with three main peaks at 2θ=43.54°, 50.61° and 74.25°, corresponding to the planes (111), (200) and (220) related to the fcc (face-centered cubic structure) of Cu metal. Moreover, two peaks are observed at 2θ=36.76° and 58.64°, corresponding to CuO whose presence was evidenced also by EDX and XPS.
These characterization data show the presence of CuO and Cu, but not of Cu2O. Moreover, no relevant changes were observed among the different samples (not reported for conciseness). This indicates that no correlation between CuO/Cu ratio and nano-morphology or fractal dimension exists. A similar situation has been observed for Fe-based electrocatalysts.

sections.heading: 3.3. Electrocatalytic tests
sections.text:
The samples described before were tested in the CO2 electrocatalytic reduction in the device described in Supplementary Information. Fig. 5a shows the carbon production rates obtained for Cu-CFx samples. Tests were carried out by applying −1.5 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) on the working electrode.
Formic acid was the main liquid product formed in these tests, with a maximum production rate of about 8 μmol h−1 for the Cu-CF2. The main gaseous carbon products were, instead, CO and CH4, but they were detected only for Cu-CF2, with a production rate of 11.5 and 2.2 μmol h−1, respectively. The presence of a dendritic structure (associated with the fractal dimension), not observed for Cu-CF1 and CuCF4, plays thus a key role in improving the catalytic performance, not only increasing the overall carbon production rate, but also changing the product distribution and the pathways of CO2 electrocatalytic conversion. Fig. 5a also shows the current density (mA cm−2) and metallic surface area profiles for all samples. The metallic surface areas have been estimated by a simple geometrical model and reported per
Fig. 2. a,b) SEM images (top-view) at different magnifications of a Cu electrocatalyst grown by electrodeposition (2min) on a Fe-Cr-Ni substrate (Cu-FCN2). SEM (top-view, c and cross-section, d) images of Cu electrocatalyst on Al grid at 2min electrodeposition time (Cu-AG2).
unit of electrode geometrical surface area. Cu-CF2 shows the highest values of both current density and metallic area. This could explain the higher production rate to formic acid for this sample. Fig. 5b shows the productivity to formic acid normalized per current density, which depends on the number of active sites for the electron transfer once fixed the other parameters. The normalized formic acid productivity is around 0.2 μmol h−1 mA−1 for Cu-CF2 and Cu-CF4 and about half for Cu-CF1. However, by considering the low activity of Cu-CF1 sample with an experimental error in the determination of both the productivity to formic acid and the current density (resulting in about± 0.15 μmol h−1 mA−1 in determining the formic acid normalized production, we may suggest that the normalized production of formic acid is similar in all the three samples, indicating thus that the same active centres for the formation of formic acid exist in all the samples. However, Cu-CF2 differs from the others for the presence of new active centres responsible for the change of selectivity towards CO and CH4. These can be associated to the fractal dimension, i.e. the dendritic structure, and it is well consistent with the observation that the fractal dimension for nanometric MoS2-type catalysts determines the catalytic
Fig. 3. a,b) SEM images (a-top view, b-cross-section) of Cu electrocatalysts grown on carbon-based GDL by 2min electrodeposition (Cu-GDL2). c, d) SEM images (topview) of c) Cu electrocatalysts electrodeposited on carbon-based GDL in 30 s (Cu-GDL0.5) and d) of Fe electrocatalysts on carbon-based GDL in 45 s (Fe-GDL0.75).
behaviour due to the formation of smoother edges and denser surfaces [24].
The collapse of the dendritic structure (for the long electrodeposition time of 4min) destroys these active sites specific for CO and CH4 formation, even though the current density remains quite high (only slightly lower than the current density for Cu-CF2). Thus, the electrodeposition time is the key synthetic parameter to control the nanostructure and fractal dimension of these Cu electrocatalysts, which is responsible for the creation of the specific sites to convert CO2 to CO and CH4. This also suggests that these sites form through different reaction paths and type of active sites than those for formic acid production.
In addition, acetic acid was also produced, especially for Cu-CF2 (see Supporting Information). Even if the reaction mechanism is still matter of discussion, there is a general agreement that formic acid is produced by a different route with respect to CO, CH4 and acetic acid [12,58,59]. In principle, the formation of formic acid does not need the presence of a specific catalyst [60], while the formation of CeC bonds requires the activation of CO2 by proper catalytic sites. The comparison of the Cu-CF2 with Cu-CF4 results indicates that the formic acid production rate was about the same, but the dendritic structure (observed only for Cu-CF2) promotes the formation of both gaseous and other liquid products (such as ethanol, acetic acid and isopropanol). Acetic acid can be formed by the reaction between the generated radical anion CO2−% and the adsorbed species eCH3, which is favoured by a high CO2 concentration or pressure [12–61]. Recently, Huan et al. obtained mainly formate by testing porous dendritic copper in CO2 electro-reduction under similar potential conditions but in the presence of an ionic liquid electrolyte [45]. However, they did not observe any of other higher carbon-chain products (like acetic acid) under these conditions. Dutta et al. reported 55% Faradaic efficiencies towards C2
products on mesoporous Cu foams formed by a template-assisted electrodeposition process [62]. They attributed the Cu foam activation to the in-situ reduction of a Cu2O phase, thereby creating a large abundance of surface sites active for CeC coupling. They also reported the formation of carbon monoxide and ethane, in accordance to our results. We feel that the formation of smoother edges and denser surfaces, due to the fractal dimension, is likely a better interpretation, which could deserve further studies to be fully demonstrated. To our knowledge, however, the present results show for the first time how the fractal-type nano-dimension is of great importance in determining both activity and selectivity in CO2 electrocatalytic reduction for samples where no other factors (impurities, other elements, etc.) could mask the results, remarking the relevance of further studies in this area.

sections.heading: 3.4. Influence of the substrate
sections.text:
Fig. 6 shows the carbon production rate obtained for Cu electrocatalysts grown on different substrates. All these electrocatalysts were prepared by 2min electrodeposition, while the CO2 reduction tests were carried out by applying −1.5 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) on the working electrode. The use of Al as the substrate (Cu-AG2) leads to an improved formation of acetic acid, but the production of CO and especially CH4 is drastically reduced. However, this sample does not show the presence of a dendritic nano-morphology (see Fig. 2c and d). Therefore, the possibility to form products involving CeC bond formation as acetic acid seems not associated with the presence of this fractal morphology, differently from the formation of gaseous products such as CO and CH4 as commented before.
On the contrary, if Cu grows on a Fe substrate (Cu-FF2), CO and CH4 become the dominant products, but productivity is obtained on Fe-CrNi as substrate (Cu-FCN2), with an overall carbon productivity of
Fig. 5. a) Carbon production rate (μmol h−1), density current (mA cm−2) and metallic surface area (normalized per unit of electrode geometrical surface area, cm2∙ cm−2) of Cu-CFx electrodes. b) Formic acid production rate normalized per unit of current (μmol h−1 mA−1) for the same samples. Testing conditions: −1.5 V (vs. Ag/AgCl); 0.5 M KHCO3, 10mLmin−1 CO2 flow.
44.6 μmol h−1, or 313 μmol h−1 cm−2 per gram of catalyst. Formic acid and CO are the main products. In this case, a highly dense dendritic structure is present, as shown in Fig. 2a and b.
In Supporting Information, the production rates obtained by testing the bare substrates (without Cu electrodeposition) are also reported. Except for the Cu foil, the bare substrates are scarcely active, producing formic acid in very small amounts. Moreover, the electrodeposition of Cu largely promotes the activity, and even for the Cu foil, significantly changes the product distribution.

sections.heading: 3.5. Improving carbon faradaic efficiency
sections.text:
Hydrogen production due to the parasitic side reaction of H+/e− recombination (in contrast to their use for CO2 reduction) was high at the applied potential of −1.5 V (vs. Ag/AgCl) for all tested catalysts grown onto metal-based substrates (see Supporting Information). For these samples, the Faradaic Efficiencies (FE) towards carbon products
were never higher than 10%. In order to limit the hydrogen production, the onset of reduction was evaluated by cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests, whose selected profiles are reported in Fig. 7. The use of metallic substrates is itself responsible for this side reaction of H2 formation. For this reason, these CV experiments were carried out by investigating Cu and Fe electrocatalysts grown onto carbon-based GDL substrates, thus avoiding the influence of H2 production from a metallic substrate. Ti was also used as substrate, because characterized from a low rate of H2 evolution reaction with respect to Cu or Fe as substrates [63]. Electrodeposition of iron was made starting from two iron precursors: FeSO4 (FeII) or Fe2(SO4)3 (FeIII). These samples are indicated as Fe(II)-Ti and Fe(III)-Ti, respectively.
All the CV scans show several reduction peaks, mainly due to the changes in the oxidation state of Cu (from CuII to CuI and from CuI to Cu0) and Fe (from FeIII to FeII and from FeII to FeI). The voltage related to the first cathodic peak (indicated by an arrow on the graphs) was
chosen to perform further amperometric tests (at lower potential than −1.5 V).
Fig. 8 shows the Faradaic Efficiency (%) towards carbon products, obtained by testing the Cu and Fe electrodeposited on different substrates at the corresponding onset potentials, reported on the right part of the Figure. In other words, the tests were carried out at the voltage V (vs. Ag/AgCl) of the first cathodic peak in the CV.
As it can be observed, the best carbon FE values were obtained with Fe electrocatalysts showing total carbon FE higher than 90%. For both Fe-GDL0.75 and Fe(III)-Ti a quite low overpotential of CO2 reduction is observed, although the minimum value (−0.3 V) is shown by CuGDL0.5 showing also the higher specific FE to formic acid, close to 60%. Total carbon selectivity of this sample is also good, over 80%, with acetic acid and CO as other products.
The tests with Cu- and Fe-GDL are directly comparable, because carried out under similar potential conditions (−0.30 and −0.35 V, respectively). The overall Carbon Faradaic Efficiencies are 82.8 and 92.0%, respectively. The Faradaic selectivity towards acetic acid (27.2 vs. 13.2%, respectively) and CO (20.3 vs. 11.6%, respectively) was higher for Fe-GDL with respect to Cu-GDL, while the contrary for formic acid FE. This result further confirms the previous observation that the presence of a fractal dimension, e.g. a dendritic-type structure, creates sites for CO formation. This role in acetic acid formation, e.g. CeC bond formation, seems to be also promoted, but as commented before, unequivocal observations have not been made in this respect. It may be also commented that even if differences could be observed between Fe and Cu as electrocatalysts, they appear to be related more to the nanostructure rather than the nature of the metal itself.
The highest carbon FE of 94.5% was obtained on Fe(III)-Ti, with only 4.5% of FE towards hydrogen. This can be ascribed to the coexistence of a dendritic morphology with a mesoporous structure within macropores higher than 1.5–2.0 μm (see Supplementary Information). However, this electrocatalysts is less selective to formic acid, instead showing the highest selectivity to CO among those tested.
As discussed in the introduction, there are no studies about CO2 electrocatalytic reduction with Fe as electrocatalysts, thus only the behaviour of Cu electrocatalysts can be compared with other results reported in literature. Sen et al. reported a maximum of Faradaic yield of HCOOH up to 29% with dendritic copper nanofoams at −1.1 V (where H2, HCOOH and CO are the main products), by making thicker the foams when the electrodeposition time (until 60 s) increases [42]. However, the authors did not report the formation of products involving the formation of CeC bonds and no correlation of the electrochemical behaviour with the foam nanostructure was reported. Kas et al. reported the behaviour of copper hollow fibre electrodes for CO2 reduction, with FE up to 85% at −0.4 V vs RHE [43]. The main products were CO (about 70% FE) and formic acid (about 15% FE), while no formation of acetic acid or other products associated to the formation of CeC bonds was observed, even if the same authors recently communicated higher Faradaic Efficiency towards ethylene and other small hydrocarbons over rough copper surface electrodes [64]. They obtained these results by maintaining low the electrolyte concentration (thus controlling the buffer capacity) and increasing the CO2 pressures to enhance the local concentration of the reactants. Similar results about the importance of maintaining high the local CO2 concentration were earlier reported by our research group [20]. In this case, the increase of CO2 concentration locally at the electrode surface was obtained by combining the presence of MOF materials with a gas-phase configuration (electrolyte-less) of the electrochemical device.
Thus, the Cu and Fe NFs prepared and tested in this work evidenced a much higher Faradaic efficiency with respect to most of the results reported in literature until now. As mentioned, Fe-based electrocatalysts with analogous nanomorphology of those tested here have not been earlier reported in literature, but the results presented in Fig. 8 indicate that they are a promising type of electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction.
A time-dependent study was also performed with Cu-FCN2 (see Supplementary Information). The amounts (μmol) of the detected products (formic acid, acetic, acid, CO and H2) all increased in 4.5 h testing time, evidencing a quite good linearity and confirming that these products were formed by different reaction routes.
Moreover, some stability tests were carried out with Fe-Ti until 20 h and the working electrode was reused a second time. The fuel productivity was found to be steadily increasing with time and the reused electrode showed only a slight loss of about 5–10% in products indicating the stability and long-term usage of the NF-based electrodes.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
Copper and iron electrocatalysts with different dendritic-type nanodimension were grown onto different substrates (Cu, Fe, Fe-Cr-Ni, Al, Ti, GDL) by an electrodeposition technique and then tested in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2. The nano-morphology strongly depends on the electrodeposition time and the nature of the substrate. SEM analysis evidenced that the nano-morphology, with the formation of a dendritic-type electrocatalyst at the intermediate time of deposition (2min), depends on the electrodeposition-time. For Fe electrocatalysts deposited on GDL or Ti, an optimized electrodeposition time of 30–45 s is instead needed to form a dendritic-type nano-morphology. Thus, a precise control on the structure/morphology of the electrocatalyst was obtained during the synthesis by modulating the electrodeposition time in the range 30 s–4min, depending on the nature of the depositing active metal (i.e. Cu or Fe).
We have introduced the concept that fractal dimension is a unifying element to describe the different nanostructures obtained by electrodeposition, ranging from dendritic-type to nanofoams. We have used this concept to estimate the surface area and describe the different type of nanostructures with the related formation of characteristics nanomorphologies, such as smoother edges and denser surfaces typical of the fractal dimension. However, being this fractal dimension describing a nanodimension still larger with respect to the molecular dimension of the active sites, it is not correct to try to made a correlation with a parameter describing the fractal dimension and the catalytic behavior, particularly when dealing on selectivity in the electrocatalytic reduction of CO2.
The results from CO2 reduction tests showed the role of a fractal dimension related to the presence of a dendritic structure, not only in enhancing the sites of electron transfer responsible for formic acid formation (higher current density and reaction rate), but also in creating new active sites responsible for the reaction pathway towards the formation of gas products (such as CO and CH4). These sites are different from those responsible for formic acid and are likely due to the formation of smoother edges and denser surfaces associated with the fractal dimension.
In a second series of experiments, cyclic voltammetry (CV) scans were used to evaluate the onset potential of the reduction reaction for Cu and Fe electrocatalysts deposited on a carbon-based gas diffusion layer (GDL) and a Ti substrate, in order to minimize the side reaction of H2 production. The results showed very high total carbon FEs for Febased electrocatalysts grown both on GDL and on metallic Ti, reaching values ranging between 92–95% and substantially reducing the formation of hydrogen. It is worth noting that this type of Fe-based electrocatalysts were not earlier reported for CO2 reduction, but the present data indicate that they are quite promising materials for further studies. The onset potential for CO2 reduction is also quite interesting, although the best value (−0.3 V) was observed for Cu electrodeposited on GDL, showing a high total carbon FE (over 80%) and especially the best specific FE to formic acid (close to 60%).
These results are very attractive with respect to those reported in literature, evidencing that the nano-morphology and fractal dimension of the electrocatalyst, rather than its chemical nature only or the presence of specific crystalline planes, is a main factors controlling the
electrocatalytic behaviour in CO2 reduction, including selectivity. To our knowledge this is an original result which could stimulate further studies and ways to improve further the catalytic behaviour, offering a new clue to control both the activity and the selectivity.
